theory.intro: A power is a short way of writing repeated multiplication, so writing powers in expanded form shows exactly why the index laws work.
facts: For a positive whole-number index $m$, $a^{m}$ means $m$ factors of $a$ multiplied together, so $3^{4}=3\times3\times3\times3$.
Expanding a product of two powers of the same base and counting the factors gives $a^{m}\times a^{n}=a^{m+n}$.
For a nonzero base $a$, expanding a quotient and cancelling matching factors gives $a^{m}\div a^{n}=a^{m-n}$. Here we use positive whole-number indices with $m>n$, so factors remain on top.
Expanding a power of a power gives $n$ copies of $m$ factors, so $\left(a^{m}\right)^{n}=a^{m\times n}$.
The multiplication and division laws require the **same base**. They do not combine powers that are added or subtracted.
steps: Write each power in expanded form.
Count the factors of the base that are left.
Write the result in index form and compare the index with the ones you started with.

workedExamples.question_text:
(a) Expand $4^{2}\times4^{3}$ and write the product as a single power.
(b) State the multiplication rule in words and algebraically.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) $4^{2}\times4^{3}$
$=(4\times4)\times(4\times4\times4)$
$=4^{5}$.
There are $2+3=5$ factors of $4$. The base stays $4$.
(b) When multiplying powers of the same base, keep the base and add the indices.
$a^{m}\times a^{n}=a^{m+n}$ for positive whole-number indices $m$ and $n$.

workedExamples.question_text:
(a) Expand $5^{5}\div5^{2}$ as a fraction, cancel matching factors and write the result as a single power.
(b) State the division rule in words and algebraically.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) $5^{5}\div5^{2}$
$=\frac{5\times5\times5\times5\times5}{5\times5}$.
Cancel two matching factors from the top and bottom. Three factors remain on top.
$=5\times5\times5$
$=5^{3}$.
(b) When dividing powers of the same nonzero base, keep the base and subtract the indices.
$a^{m}\div a^{n}=a^{m-n}$, where $a\ne0$.
Here $m>n$, so cancelling leaves a positive whole-number index.

workedExamples.question_text:
(a) Expand $\left(3^{2}\right)^{4}$ and write it as a single power.
(b) State the power-of-a-power rule in words and algebraically.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) The outer index $4$ means four groups, each containing two factors of $3$.
$\left(3^{2}\right)^{4}$
$=(3\times3)\times(3\times3)\times(3\times3)\times(3\times3)$
$=3^{8}$.
(b) When raising a power to another power, keep the base and multiply the indices.
$\left(a^{m}\right)^{n}=a^{m\times n}$ for positive whole-number indices $m$ and $n$.

workedExamples.question_text:
Which expressions can be combined using the index law of multiplication? Explain using expanded form.
(a) $7^{2}\times7$
(b) $7^{2}+7$
(c) $7^{2}\times2^{2}$
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) $7^{2}\times7=(7\times7)\times7=7^{3}$.
The last $7$ is one factor, so the indices add: $2+1=3$.
(b) $7^{2}+7=(7\times7)+7$. This adds two amounts; it does not join the factors into one product. The multiplication law does not apply.
(c) $7^{2}\times2^{2}=(7\times7)\times(2\times2)$. The bases differ, so this same-base multiplication law does not apply.

workedExamples.question_text:
A student writes $2^{2}\times2^{3}=4^{5}$.
Use expanded form to identify the error and give the correct single power.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$2^{2}\times2^{3}$
$=(2\times2)\times(2\times2\times2)$
$=2^{5}$.
The student added the indices correctly but also multiplied the bases. All five factors are still $2$, so the base stays $2$.

workedExamples.question_text:
Write $\left(2^{3}\right)^{2}$ as a product of equal powers and use the multiplication law.
Explain why it gives the same result as $\left(2^{2}\right)^{3}$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\left(2^{3}\right)^{2}=2^{3}\times2^{3}=2^{3+3}=2^{6}$.
There are two groups of three factors.
$\left(2^{2}\right)^{3}=2^{2}\times2^{2}\times2^{2}=2^{2+2+2}=2^{6}$.
There are three groups of two factors.
Both contain six factors of $2$. Repeated addition gives the same count as multiplying the inner and outer indices.

foundation.question_text:
Write $5^{2}\times 5^{7}$ in expanded form, then write the result as a single power.
Say how the index of the answer is related to $2$ and $7$.
foundation.solution_text:
$5^{2}\times 5^{7}$
$=(5\times5)\times(5\times5\times5\times5\times5\times5\times5)$
$=5^{9}$
There are $2+7=9$ factors of $5$, so the indices add.

foundation.question_text: Write $2^{3}\times 2^{2}$ in expanded form and use it to write the product as a single power.
foundation.solution_text:
$2^{3}\times 2^{2}$
$=(2\times2\times2)\times(2\times2)$
$=2^{5}$
The $3$ factors and the $2$ factors give $3+2=5$ factors of $2$.

foundation.question_text: Write $3^{6}\div 3^{2}$ as an expanded fraction, cancel, and write the result as a single power.
foundation.solution_text:
$3^{6}\div 3^{2}$
$=\frac{3\times3\times3\times3\times3\times3}{3\times3}$
$=3\times3\times3\times3$
$=3^{4}$
Cancelling removes $2$ of the $6$ factors, so the indices subtract.

foundation.question_text: Write $2^{5}\div 2^{3}$ as an expanded fraction, cancel, and write the result as a single power.
foundation.solution_text:
$2^{5}\div 2^{3}$
$=\frac{2\times2\times2\times2\times2}{2\times2\times2}$
$=2\times2$
$=2^{2}$
The $3$ factors on the bottom cancel $3$ of the $5$ on top, leaving $5-3=2$.

foundation.question_text: Write $\left(2^{2}\right)^{3}$ in expanded form and use it to write the result as a single power.
foundation.solution_text:
$\left(2^{2}\right)^{3}$
$=(2\times2)\times(2\times2)\times(2\times2)$
$=2^{6}$
There are $3$ groups of $2$ factors, so the indices multiply.

foundation.question_text: Complete the rule in words, then write it algebraically: when multiplying two powers with the same base, ......... the indices.
foundation.solution_text:
When multiplying two powers with the same base, add the indices.
$a^{m}\times a^{n}=a^{m+n}$

foundation.question_text: Explain why the index law of multiplication cannot be used to write $5^{4}\times 3^{7}$ as a single power.
foundation.solution_text:
$5^{4}\times 3^{7}$
$=(5\times5\times5\times5)\times(3\times3\times3\times3\times3\times3\times3)$
The factors are not all the same number, so they cannot be counted as one base. The law needs the same base, so these powers cannot be combined using this same-base law.

development.question_text: Write $\left(3^{3}\right)^{4}$ in expanded form and use it to write the result as a single power.
development.solution_text:
$\left(3^{3}\right)^{4}$
$=(3\times3\times3)\times(3\times3\times3)\times(3\times3\times3)\times(3\times3\times3)$
$=3^{12}$
There are $4$ groups of $3$ factors, and $3\times4=12$.

development.question_text: Write $2^{4}\times 2^{3}\times 2$ in expanded form and use it to write the product as a single power.
development.solution_text:
$2^{4}\times 2^{3}\times 2$
$=(2\times2\times2\times2)\times(2\times2\times2)\times(2)$
$=2^{8}$
A base written with no index counts as one factor, so $4+3+1=8$.

development.question_text:
A student writes $3^{2}\times 3^{4}=9^{6}$.
Use expanded form to show the correct single power.
development.solution_text:
$3^{2}\times 3^{4}$
$=(3\times3)\times(3\times3\times3\times3)$
$=3^{6}$
Every factor is still a $3$, so the base stays $3$. Only the number of factors changes.

development.question_text: Write $4^{5}\div 4^{4}$ as an expanded fraction, cancel, and write the result as a single power.

The expansion of $7^{5}\div 7^{2}$ leaves $7\times7\times7$.
Complete the rule in words, then write it algebraically: when dividing two powers with the same base, ......... the indices.
development.solution_text:
When dividing two powers with the same base, subtract the indices.
$a^{m}\div a^{n}=a^{m-n}$
The base $a$ must be nonzero.

development.question_text: Explain why the index law of division cannot be used to write $11^{3}\div 5^{2}$ as a single power.
development.solution_text:
$11^{3}\div 5^{2}$
$=\frac{11\times11\times11}{5\times5}$
No factor on the bottom matches a factor on the top, so nothing cancels. The law needs the same base, so these powers cannot be combined using this same-base law.

development.question_text:
A student writes $\left(2^{3}\right)^{2}=2^{5}$.
Use expanded form to show why the indices multiply rather than add here.
development.solution_text:
$\left(2^{3}\right)^{2}$
$=(2\times2\times2)\times(2\times2\times2)$
$=2^{6}$
The outer index says how many **groups** of $3$ factors there are, so the count is $3\times2=6$, not $3+2=5$.

mastery.question_text:
A student writes $5^{3}\times 5^{2}=25^{5}$.
Use expanded form to identify the error and give the correct single power.
mastery.solution_text:
$5^{3}\times 5^{2}$
$=(5\times5\times5)\times(5\times5)$
$=5^{5}$
The student added the indices correctly but also multiplied the two bases. Expanding shows there are still only $5$s being multiplied, so the base stays $5$.

mastery.question_text: Use expanded form to explain why $\left(2^{3}\right)^{4}$ and $\left(2^{4}\right)^{3}$ give the same single power.
mastery.solution_text:
$\left(2^{3}\right)^{4}$
$=(2\times2\times2)\times(2\times2\times2)\times(2\times2\times2)\times(2\times2\times2)$
$=2^{12}$
$\left(2^{4}\right)^{3}$
$=(2\times2\times2\times2)\times(2\times2\times2\times2)\times(2\times2\times2\times2)$
$=2^{12}$
One is $4$ groups of $3$ factors and the other is $3$ groups of $4$ factors, but both contain the same $12$ factors of $2$, because $3\times4=4\times3$.

mastery.question_text:
Write $\left(3^{2}\right)^{3}$ as a product of three equal powers, then apply the index law of multiplication to it.
Explain what this shows about the two laws.
mastery.solution_text:
$\left(3^{2}\right)^{3}$
$=3^{2}\times 3^{2}\times 3^{2}$
$=3^{2+2+2}$
$=3^{6}$
Adding the index $2$ three times gives the same count as $2\times3$, so the power-of-a-power law comes straight from the multiplication law.

mastery.question_text: Use expanded form to explain why the multiplication law combines $3^{2}\times3^{4}$ as a single power but does not combine $3^{2}+3^{4}$ in this way.
mastery.solution_text:
$3^{2}\times 3^{4}$
$=(3\times3)\times(3\times3\times3\times3)$
$=3^{6}$
$3^{2}+3^{4}$
$=(3\times3)+(3\times3\times3\times3)$
$=9+81$
$=90$
Multiplying joins the factors into one longer string of $3$s, so they can be counted as one index. Adding keeps two separate amounts rather than joining the factors into a product, so the multiplication law does not apply.
